heart.title: Human heart
heart.summary: Four chambers, four valves, the heart strings, and every vessel that carries blood in and out — from a real human scan.
heart.credit: Heart and vessels: Human Reference Atlas (HuBMAP), Visible Human Male, CC BY 4.0.
heart.info.right_atrium.desc: The right atrium collects oxygen-poor blood coming back from the body through the two venae cavae, and from the heart muscle itself through the coronary sinus. When it contracts, it pushes this blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
heart.info.right_atrium.fact: Its wall holds the sinoatrial (SA) node — the heart's natural pacemaker that starts every heartbeat.
heart.info.left_atrium.desc: The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
heart.info.left_atrium.fact: It is the chamber closest to your back — it sits right in front of the oesophagus, the tube that carries food to your stomach.
heart.info.right_ventricle.desc: The right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs. The lungs are close by, so its wall is thinner than the left ventricle’s.
heart.info.right_ventricle.fact: Seen from the front, most of the heart's front surface is actually the right ventricle.
heart.info.left_ventricle.desc: The left ventricle is the heart's main pump. It pushes oxygen-rich blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the whole body. It also forms the heart's tip, the apex.
heart.info.left_ventricle.fact: Its wall is about three times thicker than the right ventricle’s, because it has to push blood all the way to your toes.
heart.info.septum.desc: The septum is the muscular wall between the left and right ventricles. It keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood apart and helps both ventricles squeeze.
heart.info.septum.fact: Special conducting fibres run along it, spreading the electrical signal that makes both ventricles contract together.
heart.info.tricuspid_valve.desc: The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle. Its three flaps open to let blood into the ventricle, then shut so blood cannot flow back when the ventricle contracts.
heart.info.tricuspid_valve.fact: Closing valves make the sounds of your heartbeat: the first sound, the 'lub', is the tricuspid and mitral valves shutting.
heart.info.mitral_valve.desc: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle. It has only two flaps, so it is also called the bicuspid valve.
heart.info.mitral_valve.fact: It is named after a bishop's mitre (hat), because its two flaps look like one.
heart.info.pulmonary_valve.desc: The pulmonary valve guards the exit of the right ventricle. It opens when the ventricle pushes blood into the pulmonary trunk, then closes so the blood cannot fall back.
heart.info.pulmonary_valve.fact: When it closes together with the aortic valve, it makes the second heart sound — the 'dub'.
heart.info.aortic_valve.desc: The aortic valve sits at the exit of the left ventricle. It opens to let blood rush into the aorta and closes between beats so blood doesn't leak back.
heart.info.aortic_valve.fact: The openings of the heart's own coronary arteries sit just above its flaps.
heart.info.papillary_muscles.desc: Papillary muscles are small pillars of muscle inside the ventricles. Thin cords called chordae tendineae tie them to the flaps of the tricuspid and mitral valves (the cords are too fine to appear in this model).
heart.info.papillary_muscles.fact: They tighten as the ventricles squeeze, so the valve flaps can’t flip backwards — like ropes holding a sail.
heart.info.aorta.desc: The aorta is the body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle, curves over the heart in the aortic arch, then runs down through the chest and belly. Branches from the arch supply the head and arms.
heart.info.aorta.fact: In adults it is about as wide as a garden hose — roughly 2.5 to 3 cm across.
heart.info.pulmonary_trunk.desc: The pulmonary trunk is the short, wide vessel leaving the right ventricle. After about 5 cm it splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries, which carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
heart.info.pulmonary_trunk.fact: The pulmonary arteries are the only arteries in an adult that carry oxygen-poor blood.
heart.info.superior_vena_cava.desc: The superior vena cava is a large vein that brings oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest into the right atrium.
heart.info.superior_vena_cava.fact: Unlike many veins in your arms and legs, it has no valve where it opens into the heart.
heart.info.inferior_vena_cava.desc: The inferior vena cava is the body's largest vein. It carries oxygen-poor blood from the legs, belly and lower body up into the right atrium.
heart.info.inferior_vena_cava.fact: It runs up beside the aorta, on the right side of the spine.
heart.info.right_coronary_artery.desc: The right coronary artery also begins just above the aortic valve. It runs in the groove between the right atrium and the right ventricle and supplies the right side of the heart.
heart.info.right_coronary_artery.fact: In most people it also supplies the SA node, the heart's pacemaker.
heart.hint.septum: The septum is the base of the heart model.
heart.hint.ventricle: The ventricles are built around the septum — place the septum first.

heart.hint.left_atrium: The left atrium sits above the left ventricle — place the left ventricle first.
heart.hint.papillary_muscles: Papillary muscles grow from the inner walls of the ventricles — place both ventricles first.
heart.hint.tricuspid_valve: The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, held by the chordae — place the right atrium and the chordae first.
heart.hint.mitral_valve: The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle, held by the chordae — place the left atrium and the chordae first.
heart.hint.pulmonary_valve: This valve guards the exit of the right ventricle — place the right ventricle first.
heart.hint.aortic_valve: This valve guards the exit of the left ventricle — place the left ventricle first.
heart.hint.pulmonary_trunk: The pulmonary trunk starts at the pulmonary valve — place the valve first.
heart.hint.aorta: The aorta starts at the aortic valve — place the valve first.
heart.hint.vena_cava: The venae cavae empty into the right atrium — place the right atrium first.
heart.hint.coronary_artery: The coronary arteries start in the aortic root, just above the aortic valve — place the aortic valve first.
heart.info.chordae_tendineae.desc: The chordae tendineae are thin, strong cords that tie the papillary muscles to the edges of the tricuspid and mitral valve flaps. They stop the flaps flipping back into the atria when the ventricles squeeze. The scan does not include them, so they are drawn in here.
heart.info.chordae_tendineae.fact: They are often called the heart strings. They are made mostly of collagen, the same protein that makes tendons tough.
heart.info.right_pulmonary_artery.desc: The right pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood from the pulmonary trunk to the right lung. It passes behind the aorta and the superior vena cava.
heart.info.right_pulmonary_artery.fact: It is longer than the left one, because the heart sits a little to the left of the middle of the chest.
heart.info.left_pulmonary_artery.desc: The left pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood from the pulmonary trunk to the left lung, arching over the left main airway.
heart.info.left_pulmonary_artery.fact: Before birth, a short channel called the ductus arteriosus joined it to the aorta, so blood could skip the lungs, which were not breathing yet.
heart.info.pulmonary_vein.desc: Each pulmonary vein brings freshly oxygenated blood from part of a lung back into the left atrium. There are four: an upper and a lower vein from each lung.
heart.info.pulmonary_vein.fact: They are the only veins in an adult that carry oxygen-rich blood.
heart.info.brachiocephalic_artery.desc: The first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It soon splits into the right common carotid artery, for the right side of the head and brain, and the right subclavian artery, for the right arm.
heart.info.brachiocephalic_artery.fact: Its name means 'arm-head', because it supplies both.
heart.info.left_common_carotid_artery.de: The second branch of the aortic arch. It runs up the left side of the neck to supply the left side of the head and brain.
heart.info.left_common_carotid_artery.fa: This is the pulse you can feel at the side of your neck, just under the jaw.
heart.info.left_subclavian_artery.desc: The third branch of the aortic arch. It runs under the collarbone to supply the left arm, and sends a branch up to the brain.
heart.info.left_main_coronary_artery.des: The left main coronary artery starts in the aortic root, just above the aortic valve. After a short run it divides into branches that feed most of the left ventricle and the septum.
heart.info.left_main_coronary_artery.fac: Even though the heart is full of blood, its muscle can't take oxygen from the blood inside it. It relies on these arteries.
heart.info.left_anterior_descending_arte: The LAD runs down the front of the heart in the groove over the septum. It feeds the front of the left ventricle and most of the septum.
Because it feeds so much of the main pump, doctors call a sudden blockage here the 'widow-maker'.
heart.info.diagonal_branches.desc: Diagonal branches leave the LAD at an angle and cross the side of the left ventricle, bringing oxygen-rich blood to its outer wall.
heart.info.diagonal_branches.fact: Most people have one to three diagonal branches; the number varies from person to person.
heart.info.left_marginal_branch.desc: The left marginal branch runs down the rounded left edge of the heart and supplies the side wall of the left ventricle.
heart.info.left_marginal_branch.fact: It is also called the obtuse marginal artery, after the heart's rounded ('obtuse') left edge.
heart.info.right_marginal_artery.desc: The right marginal artery branches off the right coronary artery and runs along the sharp lower edge of the heart, feeding the right ventricle.
heart.info.right_marginal_artery.fact: It follows the heart's 'acute margin', the sharp edge between its front and bottom surfaces.
heart.info.posterior_descending_artery.d: The posterior descending artery runs down the back of the heart in the groove over the septum. It feeds the back of both ventricles and part of the septum.
heart.info.posterior_descending_artery.f: In about 8 out of 10 people it comes from the right coronary artery. Doctors call that a 'right-dominant' heart.
heart.info.coronary_sinus.desc: The coronary sinus is a wide vein on the back of the heart. It collects used blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium.
heart.info.coronary_sinus.fact: A small flap called the Thebesian valve guards its opening into the right atrium.
heart.info.great_cardiac_vein.desc: The great cardiac vein starts near the tip of the heart, runs up beside the LAD, then curves around the left side to drain into the coronary sinus.
heart.info.great_cardiac_vein.fact: It runs right beside the left coronary arteries, like a return lane next to a road.
heart.info.middle_cardiac_vein.desc: The middle cardiac vein runs up the back of the heart beside the posterior descending artery and drains into the coronary sinus.
heart.info.middle_cardiac_vein.fact: The heart's veins usually run alongside its arteries, just as they do in the rest of the body.
heart.info.small_cardiac_vein.desc: The small cardiac vein runs along the lower right edge of the heart, beside the right marginal artery, and drains into the coronary sinus.
heart.info.small_cardiac_vein.fact: It is the smallest of the veins that drain into the coronary sinus, and some people don't have one.
heart.info.anterior_cardiac_veins.desc: These small veins drain the front of the right ventricle. Unlike the others, they skip the coronary sinus and open straight into the right atrium.
heart.info.anterior_cardiac_veins.fact: Even tinier veins, the Thebesian veins, drain the heart wall directly into its chambers.
heart.hint.chordae_tendineae: The cords tie the papillary muscles to the valve flaps — place the papillary muscles first.
heart.hint.pulmonary_artery: The pulmonary arteries branch off the pulmonary trunk — place the trunk first.
heart.hint.pulmonary_vein: The pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium — place the left atrium first.
heart.hint.arch_branch: This artery leaves the top of the aortic arch — place the aorta first.
heart.hint.left_anterior_descending_arte: The LAD is a branch of the left main coronary artery — place the left main first.
heart.hint.diagonal_branches: The diagonal branches come off the LAD — place the LAD first.
heart.hint.left_marginal_branch: In this scan the left marginal branch joins the diagonal branches — place them first.
heart.hint.right_branch: This artery branches off the right coronary artery — place the right coronary artery first.
heart.hint.coronary_sinus: The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium — place the right atrium first.
heart.hint.cardiac_vein: This vein drains into the coronary sinus — place the coronary sinus first.
heart.hint.anterior_cardiac_veins: These veins open straight into the right atrium — place the right atrium first.
heart.link.right_ventricle: Fit the right ventricle against the right side of the septum. It will pump oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
heart.link.left_ventricle: Fit the left ventricle against the left side of the septum. It is the heart's strongest pump, sending blood to the whole body.
heart.link.right_atrium: Set the right atrium on top of the right ventricle. Blood coming back from the body collects here before it drops into the ventricle.
heart.link.left_atrium: Set the left atrium on top of the left ventricle, at the back of the heart. Blood fresh from the lungs arrives here.
heart.link.papillary_muscles: Place the papillary muscles on the inner walls of the ventricles. They will anchor the valve cords.
heart.link.chordae_tendineae: Tie the chordae tendineae to the tips of the papillary muscles. Their other ends will hold the valve flaps.
heart.link.tricuspid_valve: Fit the tricuspid valve into the opening between the right atrium and right ventricle, so blood can only flow down.
heart.link.mitral_valve: Fit the mitral valve between the left atrium and left ventricle. It lets blood in, then snaps shut when the ventricle squeezes.
heart.link.pulmonary_valve: Put the pulmonary valve at the exit of the right ventricle. It stops blood falling back from the lungs' artery.
heart.link.aortic_valve: Put the aortic valve at the exit of the left ventricle. Every drop of blood for the body passes through it.
heart.link.superior_vena_cava: Connect the superior vena cava to the top of the right atrium. Oxygen-poor blood from your head and arms pours in here.
heart.link.inferior_vena_cava: Connect the inferior vena cava to the bottom of the right atrium. Blood from your legs and belly comes up through it.
heart.link.pulmonary_trunk: Connect the pulmonary trunk to the pulmonary valve. Oxygen-poor blood leaves the heart here on its way to the lungs.
heart.link.right_pulmonary_artery: Connect the right pulmonary artery to the pulmonary trunk. It carries blood to the right lung.
heart.link.left_pulmonary_artery: Connect the left pulmonary artery to the pulmonary trunk. It carries blood to the left lung.
heart.link.right_superior_pulmonary_vein: Connect the right upper pulmonary vein to the left atrium. Oxygen-rich blood from the top of the right lung flows in.
heart.link.right_inferior_pulmonary_vein: Connect the right lower pulmonary vein to the left atrium. Oxygen-rich blood from the bottom of the right lung flows in.
heart.link.left_superior_pulmonary_vein: Connect the left upper pulmonary vein to the left atrium. Oxygen-rich blood from the top of the left lung flows in.
heart.link.left_inferior_pulmonary_vein: Connect the left lower pulmonary vein to the left atrium. Oxygen-rich blood from the bottom of the left lung flows in.
heart.link.aorta: Connect the aorta to the aortic valve. Oxygen-rich blood leaves here for the whole body.
heart.link.brachiocephalic_artery: Connect the brachiocephalic artery to the top of the aortic arch. It feeds the right arm and the right side of the head.
heart.link.left_common_carotid_artery: Connect the left common carotid artery to the aortic arch, next to the brachiocephalic artery. It feeds the left side of the head.
heart.link.left_subclavian_artery: Connect the left subclavian artery to the far end of the aortic arch. It feeds the left arm.
heart.link.left_main_coronary_artery: Connect the left main coronary artery to the aortic root, just above the valve. This is where the heart muscle's own blood supply begins.
heart.link.left_anterior_descending_arte: Connect the LAD to the left main coronary artery, running down the front of the heart over the septum.
heart.link.diagonal_branches: Connect the diagonal branches to the LAD. They fan out across the left ventricle.
heart.link.left_marginal_branch: Connect the left marginal branch where it meets the diagonal branches. It runs down the heart's left edge.
heart.link.right_coronary_artery: Connect the right coronary artery to the aortic root. It wraps around the right side of the heart, in the groove between atrium and ventricle.
heart.link.right_marginal_artery: Connect the right marginal artery to the right coronary artery. It runs along the heart's sharp lower edge.
heart.link.posterior_descending_artery: Connect the posterior descending artery to the right coronary artery. It runs down the back of the heart.
heart.link.coronary_sinus: Connect the coronary sinus to the right atrium. Used blood from the heart muscle drains back in here.
heart.link.great_cardiac_vein: Connect the great cardiac vein to the coronary sinus. It collects blood from the front and left of the heart.
heart.link.middle_cardiac_vein: Connect the middle cardiac vein to the coronary sinus. It collects blood from the back of the heart.
heart.link.small_cardiac_vein: Connect the small cardiac vein to the coronary sinus. It collects blood from the lower right edge.
heart.link.anterior_cardiac_veins: Connect the anterior cardiac veins straight to the right atrium. They drain the front of the right ventricle.
robotDog.title: Robot dog
robotDog.summary: A real open-source quadruped: 12 motors, a computer, a battery and a laser scanner on four legs.
robotDog.credit: Robot dog based on Mini Pupper 2 by MangDang, Apache License 2.0. Servos and battery modelled by Hologemma.
robotDog.info.frame.desc: The frame is the robot's skeleton. Every other part is fixed to it, so it has to be light but stiff — the legs need something solid to push against.
robotDog.info.frame.fact: Engineers use the frame as the robot's reference point (the 'base link') when they describe where every other part is.
robotDog.info.battery.desc: The rechargeable lithium battery stores energy for the motors, the computer and the sensors. It sits low and near the middle so the weight stays balanced.
robotDog.info.battery.fact: When the robot jumps or climbs, all twelve motors pull current at once — the battery must deliver strong bursts of power, not just store energy.
robotDog.info.controller_board.desc: The main circuit board carries a small computer, power circuits and connectors. It runs the control loop: read the sensors, decide, and send new angles to every motor many times per second.
robotDog.info.controller_board.fact: It also holds an IMU (inertial measurement unit) — a tiny chip that senses tilt and acceleration, so the robot knows when it is about to fall.
robotDog.info.servos.desc: Each leg has three servo motors: one swings the leg out to the side, one swings the upper leg forward and back at the hip, and one bends the knee. A servo is a motor with gears and a sensor that can hold any angle it is told.
robotDog.info.servos.fact: Twelve servos give the robot 12 'degrees of freedom' — 3 per leg, the minimum for a foot to reach any point beneath it.
robotDog.info.hip.desc: The hip module joins the leg to the body and holds the leg's motors. It tilts the whole leg in or out to keep the robot balanced.
robotDog.info.hip.fact: Putting the heavy motors at the hip, close to the body, keeps the legs light and quick to swing.
robotDog.info.upper_leg.desc: The upper leg (thigh) swings forward and back from the hip, like your own thigh when you walk.
robotDog.info.upper_leg.fact: Robot legs are made light on purpose: the less weight at the end of a leg, the less force a motor needs to swing it.
robotDog.info.lower_leg.desc: The lower leg bends at the knee and ends in a rubber foot that grips the floor. Upper and lower leg work together like your thigh and shin.
robotDog.info.lower_leg.fact: The foot is the only part that touches the ground — the grip there is what lets the robot push itself forward.
robotDog.info.lidar.desc: LiDAR spins a laser beam and measures how long the light takes to bounce back. That builds a 360° map of distances, so the robot can avoid walls and map a room.
robotDog.info.lidar.fact: Light travels about 30 cm in one billionth of a second — LiDAR measures time that precisely.
robotDog.info.front_plate.desc: The front plate closes the body at the front and protects the electronics behind it.
robotDog.info.front_plate.fact: Covers go on last in real robot building too, so engineers can test the wiring before closing everything up.
robotDog.info.side_shells.desc: The side shells cover the body and keep dust and fingers away from the moving parts and circuits inside.
robotDog.info.side_shells.fact: A shell also stiffens the body, a bit like how an egg shell is strong for its weight.
robotDog.hint.frame: The frame is the base of the robot.

tips.title: Gestures
tips.pinchText: Turns the model. Let go and it stays exactly where you left it.
tips.pull: Pinch with both hands near the model, pull apart
tips.pullText: Takes it to pieces. Push your hands together to close it.
tips.twist: Pinch with both hands and turn them like a wheel
tips.zoom: Pinch with both hands away from the model, pull apart
tips.zoomText: Makes it bigger, like zooming on a phone. Push your hands together to make it smaller.
tips.bloom: Touch all five fingertips together, then open your hand like a flower
tips.bloomText: Makes the model bigger — the wider you open, the bigger it gets. Hold still to keep the size.
tips.gather: Hold your hand open, then close all five fingertips together
tips.gatherText: Makes the model smaller. Open again to undo; hold still to keep the size.
tips.push: Push both open palms towards the camera
tips.pushText: Resets the view: turn, size and pieces.
tips.grabText: Pick it up. Pinch with your other hand and pull away to study it.
tips.dwellText: Hold still until it fills — or pinch it.
tips.fist: Make a fist for a second
tips.mouse: Mouse: drag to turn, scroll to zoom, double-click a part to study it.
lungs.title: Human lungs
lungs.summary: Two lungs, five lobes, 18 segments and hundreds of lobules, with the airways, vessels and diaphragm — from a real human scan. Watch them breathe.
lungs.credit: Lungs, bronchi and pulmonary vessels: Human Reference Atlas (HuBMAP), Visible Human Male, CC BY 4.0. Trachea, main bronchi, diaphragm and lobules modelled by Hologemma.
lungs.info.trachea.desc: The trachea (windpipe) carries air from the larynx down into the chest, where it splits into the two main bronchi at the carina. It is about 10–12 cm long and 2 cm wide, held open by 16–20 C-shaped rings of cartilage.
lungs.info.trachea.fact: Its lining is covered in cilia that beat about 15 times a second, sweeping a layer of sticky mucus — and the dust and germs caught in it — up to your throat.
lungs.info.right_bronchial_tree.desc: From the carina, the right main bronchus divides into three lobar bronchi (upper, middle, lower) and then ten segmental bronchi, one for each segment — the real branching of this lung, from the atlas scan.
lungs.info.right_bronchial_tree.fact: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and steeper than the left, so inhaled objects such as peanuts end up on the right far more often.
lungs.info.left_bronchial_tree.desc: The left main bronchus is about 5 cm long. It runs under the aortic arch to the left lung, where it divides into the upper and lower lobar bronchi and their segmental bronchi.
lungs.info.left_bronchial_tree.fact: Before air reaches the alveoli, the airways branch about 23 times — from one trachea into roughly 8 million tiny alveolar ducts.
lungs.info.right_upper_lobe.desc: The top of the right lung. The horizontal fissure separates it from the middle lobe and the oblique fissure from the lower lobe. It has three segments: apical, posterior and anterior.
lungs.info.right_upper_lobe.fact: Its apex rises 2–3 cm above the collarbone, into the root of the neck.
lungs.info.right_middle_lobe.desc: A wedge at the front of the right lung, between the horizontal and oblique fissures, with a lateral and a medial segment. It rests against the right side of the heart.
lungs.info.right_middle_lobe.fact: Because it touches the heart, pneumonia here blurs the heart's right border on an X-ray — doctors call this the silhouette sign.
lungs.info.right_lower_lobe.desc: The largest lobe of the right lung, behind and below the oblique fissure, resting on the diaphragm. It has five segments: superior and four basal ones.
lungs.info.right_lower_lobe.fact: The lung bases move the most when you breathe in, so the lower lobes get the most fresh air with each breath — and, when you stand, the most blood too.
lungs.info.left_upper_lobe.desc: The upper lobe of the left lung, separated from the lower lobe by the oblique fissure. Its front edge has the cardiac notch, where the heart pushes the lung aside, and below it the lingula.
lungs.info.left_upper_lobe.fact: The lingula (Latin for 'little tongue') is the left lung's version of the right middle lobe.
lungs.info.left_lower_lobe.desc: The lower lobe of the left lung, behind and below the oblique fissure, resting on the left dome of the diaphragm. It has a superior segment and four basal segments.
lungs.info.left_lower_lobe.fact: Much of it lies behind the heart, so on a chest X-ray it is partly hidden in the heart's shadow.
lungs.info.pulmonary_arteries.desc: The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle and divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries. Inside the lungs their branches follow the bronchi, one artery for every segment.
lungs.info.pulmonary_arteries.fact: They are the only arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood, and their pressure is low: about 15 mmHg on average, a sixth of the pressure in the body's arteries.
lungs.info.pulmonary_veins.desc: Four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, bring freshly oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.
lungs.info.pulmonary_veins.fact: Inside the lung the veins run between the segments, not alongside the bronchi — which is why a surgeon can remove a single segment.
lungs.info.diaphragm.desc: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs and your main breathing muscle. When it contracts it flattens and moves down — about 1.5 cm in a quiet breath, up to 6–10 cm in a deep one — so the chest grows and air flows in. It is driven by the phrenic nerves (from spinal levels C3–C5).
lungs.info.diaphragm.fact: At rest it does about two-thirds of the work of breathing without you thinking about it — roughly 20,000 times a day.
lungs.hint.bronchial_tree: The bronchial trees hang from the trachea — place the trachea first.
lungs.hint.right_lobe: The lobes wrap around their bronchi — place the right bronchial tree first.
lungs.hint.left_lobe: The lobes wrap around their bronchi — place the left bronchial tree first.
lungs.hint.pulmonary_arteries: The pulmonary arteries enter each lung beside the bronchi — place both bronchial trees first.
lungs.hint.pulmonary_veins: The veins leave the hilum just below the arteries — place the pulmonary arteries first.
lungs.hint.diaphragm: The diaphragm sits under the lung bases — place both lower lobes first.
lungs.piece.right_apical.desc: The top of the right lung, rising above the first rib into the root of the neck. Supplied by the apical bronchus (B1).
lungs.piece.right_posterior.desc: The back of the upper lobe, against the upper ribs. Supplied by B2. In someone lying on their back, inhaled food or fluid often settles here.
lungs.piece.right_anterior.desc: The front of the upper lobe, behind the upper chest wall, reaching down to the horizontal fissure. Supplied by B3.
lungs.piece.right_lateral.desc: The outer half of the middle lobe, under the side of the chest. Supplied by B4.
lungs.piece.right_medial.desc: The inner half of the middle lobe, lying against the right atrium of the heart. Supplied by B5.
lungs.piece.right_superior.desc: The top of the lower lobe, at the back. Its bronchus (B6) is the first branch of the lower lobe bronchus and points straight back, so it is another common site for aspiration when lying down.
lungs.piece.right_medial_basal.desc: The smallest segment, tucked below the hilum against the heart and the inferior vena cava. Supplied by B7.
lungs.piece.right_anterior_basal.desc: The front of the lung base, resting on the diaphragm. Supplied by B8.
lungs.piece.right_lateral_basal.desc: The outer part of the base, reaching down into the costodiaphragmatic recess between the ribs and the diaphragm. Supplied by B9.
lungs.piece.right_posterior_basal.desc: The back of the base — the lowest, deepest part of the lung, reaching down behind the liver. Supplied by B10.
lungs.piece.left_apical.desc: The top of the left lung. It shares one bronchus with the posterior segment (the apicoposterior bronchus, B1+2), so many anatomists count the two as one segment.
lungs.piece.left_posterior.desc: The back of the upper lobe, also supplied by the apicoposterior bronchus (B1+2).
lungs.piece.left_anterior.desc: The front of the upper lobe, above the cardiac notch. Supplied by B3.
lungs.piece.left_superior_lingular.desc: The upper half of the lingula, the tongue-shaped lower part of the left upper lobe. Supplied by B4.
lungs.piece.left_inferior_lingular.desc: The tip of the lingula, curving over the front of the heart below the cardiac notch. Supplied by B5.
lungs.piece.left_superior.desc: The top of the left lower lobe, at the back. Supplied by B6, the first branch of the lower lobe bronchus.
lungs.piece.left_medial_basal.desc: The inner part of the base, beside the heart. On the left its bronchus often shares a stem with the anterior basal one, so the two are also described as one anteromedial segment.
lungs.piece.left_anterior_basal.desc: The front of the left lung base, on the diaphragm. Supplied by B8.
lungs.piece.left_lateral_basal.desc: The outer part of the base, in the costodiaphragmatic recess. Supplied by B9.
lungs.piece.left_posterior_basal.desc: The back of the base, the lowest part of the left lung, behind the stomach and spleen. Supplied by B10.
lungs.piece.lobule.desc: A secondary pulmonary lobule: the smallest piece of lung walled off by its own connective-tissue septa, 1–2.5 cm across. A tiny bronchiole and artery enter at its centre, veins and lymph vessels run in its walls, and inside it 3 to 24 acini — grape-like clusters of alveoli — swap oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood.
lungs.piece.cartilage_rings.desc: Sixteen to twenty C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage stacked down the trachea. They stop it from collapsing while you breathe in, but still let it bend.
lungs.piece.tracheal_ring.desc: One C-shaped ring of hyaline cartilage, open at the back. The lowest ring is shaped into the carina, the keel-like ridge between the two main bronchi.
lungs.piece.trachealis.desc: A band of smooth muscle closing the open back of every ring. When you cough it contracts, narrowing the trachea so the air blasts out faster. The oesophagus lies right behind it.
lungs.piece.annular_ligaments.desc: Fibroelastic membranes joining each ring to the next, so the trachea can stretch, bend and lengthen when you breathe in or lift your chin.
lungs.piece.mucosa.desc: The inner lining: ciliated epithelium with mucus-making goblet cells. The mucus traps dust and germs and the cilia sweep it up to the throat — the mucociliary escalator.
lungs.piece.right_main_bronchus.desc: About 2.5 cm long and 1.5 cm wide, it leaves the carina at a steep angle (about 25° from vertical) and enters the right lung at the hilum.
lungs.piece.left_main_bronchus.desc: About 5 cm long and narrower than the right, it leaves the carina at about 45°, passes under the aortic arch and in front of the oesophagus and aorta, and enters the left lung.
lungs.piece.main_bronchus_rings.desc: C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, like the trachea's, keep the main bronchus open.
lungs.piece.main_bronchus_wall.desc: The ciliated lining, the ligaments between the rings and the smooth muscle across the back.
lungs.piece.bronchial_wall.desc: The bronchial wall: a ciliated lining with mucus glands, a layer of smooth muscle that can narrow the airway (it tightens in asthma) and elastic fibres.
lungs.piece.bronchial_cartilage.desc: In the bronchi the cartilage rings break up into irregular plates. They hold the airway open while you breathe out. Airways narrower than about 1 mm — the bronchioles — have none.
lungs.piece.right_upper_lobe_bronchus.de: Leaves the right main bronchus only about 2 cm below the carina, above the right pulmonary artery (it is also called the eparterial bronchus). It splits into the apical, posterior and anterior bronchi.
The bronchus intermedius continues the right main bronchus for 2–3 cm below the upper lobe branch, then splits into the middle and lower lobe bronchi.
lungs.piece.right_middle_lobe_bronchus.d: Runs forward to the middle lobe and divides into the lateral (B4) and medial (B5) bronchi. Long, narrow and ringed by lymph nodes, it is easily blocked.
lungs.piece.right_lower_lobe_bronchus.de: Continues down into the lower lobe. It first gives off the superior bronchus (B6) backwards, then the four basal bronchi (B7–B10).
lungs.piece.right_apical_bronchus.desc: Runs up to the apical segment. Like every segmental bronchus it keeps dividing, some 15–20 more times, before the air reaches the alveoli.
lungs.piece.right_posterior_bronchus.des: Runs back and up to the posterior segment of the upper lobe.
lungs.piece.right_anterior_bronchus.desc: Runs forward to the anterior segment of the upper lobe.
lungs.piece.right_lateral_bronchus.desc: Supplies the lateral segment of the middle lobe.
lungs.piece.right_medial_bronchus.desc: Supplies the medial segment of the middle lobe, beside the heart.
lungs.piece.right_superior_bronchus.desc: The first branch of the lower lobe bronchus, pointing straight back to the superior segment.
Supplies the small medial basal segment beside the heart.
lungs.piece.right_anterior_basal_bronchu: Runs forward and down to the front of the lung base.
lungs.piece.right_lateral_basal_bronchus: Runs down and out to the lateral basal segment.
lungs.piece.right_posterior_basal_bronch: The end of the lower lobe bronchus, running down and back to the lowest part of the lung.
lungs.piece.left_upper_lobe_bronchus.des: Leaves the left main bronchus and almost at once divides into an upper branch (apicoposterior and anterior bronchi) and the lingular bronchus.
lungs.piece.left_lower_lobe_bronchus.des: Continues down into the lower lobe, giving off the superior bronchus (B6) and then the basal bronchi.
lungs.piece.left_apicoposterior_bronchus: One stem for both the apical and posterior segments, splitting into their branches higher up.
lungs.piece.left_anterior_bronchus.desc: Runs forward to the anterior segment of the upper lobe.
lungs.piece.left_lingular_bronchus.desc: The stem of the lingula, running forward and down before splitting into the superior and inferior lingular bronchi.
lungs.piece.left_superior_lingular_bronc: Supplies the upper half of the lingula.
lungs.piece.left_inferior_lingular_bronc: Supplies the tip of the lingula, over the heart.
lungs.piece.left_superior_bronchus.desc: The first branch of the left lower lobe bronchus, pointing back to the superior segment.
lungs.piece.left_medial_basal_bronchus.d: Supplies the medial basal segment beside the heart; it often shares a stem with B8.
lungs.piece.left_anterior_basal_bronchus: Runs forward and down to the front of the base.
Runs down and out to the lateral basal segment.
lungs.piece.left_posterior_basal_bronchu: Runs down and back to the lowest part of the left lung.
lungs.piece.pulmonary_trunk.desc: Carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle. About 5 cm long, it divides beneath the aortic arch into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
lungs.piece.right_pulmonary_artery.desc: The longer of the two: it runs behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava to the right hilum, then branches beside the bronchi.
lungs.piece.left_pulmonary_artery.desc: Arches over the left main bronchus to the left hilum. A small ligament, left over from a shortcut used before birth, ties it to the aorta.
lungs.piece.right_superior_vein.desc: Drains the right upper and middle lobes into the left atrium.
lungs.piece.right_inferior_vein.desc: Drains the right lower lobe into the left atrium.
lungs.piece.left_superior_vein.desc: Drains the left upper lobe, lingula included.
lungs.piece.central_tendon.desc: The three-leaved tendon at the top of the diaphragm, which all its muscle fibres pull on. The heart sits on it, and the inferior vena cava passes through it (at the T8 vertebra) — breathing in widens that opening and helps draw blood back to the heart.
lungs.piece.right_dome.desc: Muscle fibres from the lower six ribs, the sternum and the spine, rising to the central tendon. The right dome sits higher than the left, pushed up by the liver.
lungs.piece.left_dome.desc: The lower dome, over the stomach and spleen. The oesophagus passes through the muscle near it, at the T10 vertebra.
lungs.piece.right_crus.desc: A long pillar anchoring the diaphragm to the L1–L3 vertebrae. Its fibres loop around the oesophagus like a sling, helping keep stomach acid down.
lungs.piece.left_crus.desc: A shorter pillar from the L1–L2 vertebrae. Between the two crura the aorta passes behind the diaphragm, at the T12 vertebra.
lungs.tour.overview.title: Your lungs
lungs.tour.overview.text: Two spongy organs filling most of your chest, holding about 300 million alveoli with a surface of some 70 m² — about a third of a tennis court. Every lobe, segment and airway here comes from a real human scan.
lungs.tour.trachea.title: The trachea
lungs.tour.trachea.text: Air comes in through the trachea, a 10–12 cm tube held open by C-shaped cartilage rings. The open backs of the rings are closed by the trachealis muscle, right in front of the oesophagus.
lungs.tour.bronchi.title: The bronchial tree
lungs.tour.bronchi.text: At the carina the trachea splits into two main bronchi, then into a bronchus for every lobe and every segment. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and steeper than the left.
lungs.tour.right_lung.title: Right lung: three lobes
lungs.tour.right_lung.text: The right lung has upper, middle and lower lobes, separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures.
lungs.tour.left_lung.title: Left lung: two lobes
lungs.tour.left_lung.text: The left lung has only two lobes, to make room for the heart. Its front edge has the cardiac notch, and below it the tongue-shaped lingula.
lungs.tour.segments.title: Segments and lobules
lungs.tour.segments.text: Each lobe is made of bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own bronchus and artery — 18 in all here. Open a lobe (hold it and pull with your other hand) to split it into segments, then open a segment to split it into lobules, the smallest pieces of lung.
lungs.tour.vessels.title: Blood in and out
lungs.tour.vessels.text: The pulmonary arteries bring oxygen-poor blood from the heart, and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood back. They enter and leave each lung at the hilum, beside the bronchi.
lungs.tour.diaphragm.title: The diaphragm
lungs.tour.diaphragm.text: Your main breathing muscle, a dome under the lungs. The vena cava, the oesophagus and the aorta pass through it.
lungs.tour.breathe.title: A breath
lungs.tour.breathe.text: The diaphragm contracts and moves down, the lungs fill from the base, and fresh air (blue-white) flows down the airway tree. Then the lungs recoil and air carrying carbon dioxide (amber) flows out. Try a deep breath.
lungs.stageText.inhale: The diaphragm contracts and moves down and the ribs swing up and out. Pressure in the chest falls below the air outside, so air rushes in.
lungs.stageText.exhale: The diaphragm relaxes and the stretched lungs recoil like a balloon, pushing the air out. At rest this needs no muscle at all.
lungs.stageText.pause: The lungs pulling inward and the chest wall pulling outward balance out. About 2.5 litres of air stay in your lungs.
lungs.monitor.legend: Blue-white dots: fresh air going in (21% oxygen). Amber dots: air going out, with about 4% carbon dioxide and less oxygen.
lungs.monitor.fact.quiet: A quiet breath moves about 500 mL, but only about 350 mL reaches the alveoli; the rest just fills the airways (the 'dead space').
lungs.monitor.fact.deep: A deep breath can move 3 litres or more. The diaphragm drops up to 6–10 cm, and muscles in the neck and between the ribs help lift the chest.
brain.title: Human brain
brain.summary: Lobes, deep structures, cerebellum and brainstem — 283 structures from a real brain atlas, grouped into 22 parts.
brain.credit: Brain: Human Reference Atlas (HuBMAP) with Allen Human Brain Atlas structures, Visible Human Male, CC BY 4.0.
brain.info.frontal_lobe.desc: The frontal lobe sits behind your forehead. It plans, makes decisions and controls movement — its back strip, the motor cortex, sends commands to your muscles. It also helps control behaviour and emotions.
brain.info.frontal_lobe.fact: The very front part (the prefrontal cortex) is the last brain area to fully mature — often not until your mid-20s.
brain.info.parietal_lobe.desc: The parietal lobe processes touch, temperature, pain and the position of your body. It combines the senses to tell you where things are around you.
brain.info.parietal_lobe.fact: Its front strip holds a 'map' of the body — the hands and lips take up a surprisingly large part of it.
brain.info.temporal_lobe.desc: The temporal lobes, beside your ears, handle hearing, understanding language and recognising faces and objects. Together with the hippocampus they help store memories.
brain.info.temporal_lobe.fact: In most people the left temporal lobe contains Wernicke's area, which is key for understanding speech.
brain.info.occipital_lobe.desc: The occipital lobe at the back of the head is the main visual centre. It turns signals from the eyes into shapes, colours and movement.
brain.info.occipital_lobe.fact: Each side of the brain sees the opposite half of the world: the left occipital lobe processes what is to your right.
brain.info.insula.desc: The insula is a hidden lobe folded deep inside the side of the brain. It senses the body's inner state — heartbeat, hunger, pain — and links it to feelings.
brain.info.insula.fact: It contains the main taste area of the cortex, and it is active when you feel disgust.
brain.info.limbic_cortex.desc: The limbic cortex — mainly the cingulate gyrus and the parahippocampal gyrus — curves around the middle of the brain. It links emotion, attention and memory.
brain.info.limbic_cortex.fact: The cingulate gyrus becomes active when you notice you made a mistake, and when something hurts.
brain.info.hippocampus.desc: The hippocampus is a curved structure deep in the temporal lobe. It turns new experiences into long-term memories and helps you find your way. The fornix carries its signals onward.
brain.info.hippocampus.fact: Its name means 'seahorse' in Greek, because of its curled shape.
brain.info.amygdala.desc: The amygdala is an almond-shaped group of nuclei in front of the hippocampus. It detects threats, drives fear and other strong emotions, and helps emotional memories stick.
brain.info.amygdala.fact: 'Amygdala' comes from the Greek word for almond.
brain.info.basal_ganglia.desc: The basal ganglia are deep clusters of nerve cells (the caudate, putamen, globus pallidus and others). They help start smooth movements, stop unwanted ones and build habits.
brain.info.basal_ganglia.fact: Parkinson's disease happens when the dopamine cells that feed the basal ganglia, in the substantia nigra, die.
brain.info.thalamus.desc: The thalamus is the brain's relay station. Almost all signals from the senses — except smell — pass through it on their way to the cortex.
brain.info.thalamus.fact: There is one thalamus in each half of the brain, each about the size of a walnut.
brain.info.hypothalamus.desc: The hypothalamus, just below the thalamus, controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep. It also commands the pituitary gland, the body's 'master gland' for hormones.
brain.info.hypothalamus.fact: It is smaller than an almond, yet it steers much of the body's hormone system.
brain.info.corpus_callosum.desc: The corpus callosum is a thick band of about 200 million nerve fibres that connects the left and right hemispheres so they can share information.
brain.info.corpus_callosum.fact: Rarely, surgeons cut it to stop severe epilepsy; afterwards the two halves of the brain can act surprisingly independently.
brain.info.ventricles.desc: The ventricles are connected spaces filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid cushions the brain, carries away waste and keeps the chemical balance right.
brain.info.ventricles.fact: Your body makes about half a litre of this fluid every day, replacing it several times a day.
brain.info.cerebellum.desc: The cerebellum ('little brain') at the back coordinates balance, posture and smooth, precise movement. It also helps you learn movement skills like riding a bike.
brain.info.cerebellum.fact: It is only about a tenth of the brain's volume, but it holds more than half of all its neurons.
brain.info.brainstem.desc: The brainstem — midbrain, pons and medulla — connects the brain to the spinal cord. It runs automatic life functions such as breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and swallowing, and it controls sleep and waking.
brain.info.brainstem.fact: Most of the nerves of the head and face (the cranial nerves) start in the brainstem.
brain.info.olfactory_pathway.desc: The olfactory bulbs and tracts carry smell signals from the nose to the brain.
brain.info.olfactory_pathway.fact: Smell is the only sense that does not pass through the thalamus first — it goes almost straight to emotion and memory areas, which is why smells can bring back memories so strongly.
brain.info.visual_pathway.desc: The optic chiasm, optic tracts and optic radiations carry signals from the eyes to the visual cortex in the occipital lobes.
brain.info.visual_pathway.fact: At the optic chiasm, the fibres from the inner half of each eye cross over to the other side of the brain.
brain.info.pineal_gland.desc: The pineal gland is a tiny gland in the middle of the brain. It releases melatonin, the hormone that helps control your sleep–wake cycle.
brain.info.pineal_gland.fact: It makes most of its melatonin in the dark, which is why bright screens at night can delay sleep.
brain.hint.brainstem: The brainstem is the base of the brain model.
brain.hint.cerebellum: The cerebellum sits on the back of the brainstem — place the brainstem first.
brain.hint.thalamus: The thalamus sits on top of the brainstem — place the brainstem first.
brain.hint.hypothalamus: The hypothalamus sits just below the thalamus — place the thalamus first.
brain.hint.pineal_gland: The pineal gland sits at the back of the thalamus — place the thalamus first.
brain.hint.basal_ganglia: The basal ganglia lie beside the thalamus — place the thalamus first.
brain.hint.hippocampus: The hippocampus curves around the thalamus — place the thalamus first.
brain.hint.amygdala: The amygdala sits at the front tip of the hippocampus — place the hippocampus first.
brain.hint.ventricles: The ventricles wrap around the thalamus — place the thalamus first.
brain.hint.visual_pathway: The optic tracts end in the thalamus — place the thalamus first.
brain.hint.corpus_callosum: The corpus callosum forms the roof of the ventricles — place the ventricles first.
brain.hint.limbic_cortex: The cingulate gyrus wraps around the corpus callosum — place the corpus callosum first.
brain.hint.olfactory_pathway: Smell signals go to the limbic cortex — place the limbic cortex first.
brain.hint.insula: The insula lies just outside the basal ganglia — place the basal ganglia first.
brain.hint.frontal_lobe: The frontal lobes cover the deep structures — place the corpus callosum and the insula first.
brain.hint.parietal_lobe: The parietal lobe sits behind the frontal lobe — place the frontal lobe on this side first.
brain.hint.temporal_lobe: The temporal lobe covers the insula, hippocampus and amygdala — place those first.
brain.hint.occipital_lobe: The occipital lobe sits at the back, behind the parietal lobe — place the parietal lobe on this side first.
rocketEngine.title: Rocket engine
rocketEngine.summary: A liquid-fuel rocket engine: pumps, a turbine, a combustion chamber and a bell nozzle that turn kerosene and liquid oxygen into thrust.
rocketEngine.credit: Rocket engine: an original design modelled by Hologemma (gas-generator cycle, kerosene and liquid oxygen).
rocketEngine.info.combustion_chamber.des: Kerosene and liquid oxygen burn here at over 3,000 °C and very high pressure. The hot gas speeds up as it is squeezed through the narrow throat at the bottom.
rocketEngine.info.combustion_chamber.fac: The flame is hotter than the melting point of the chamber wall — the wall survives only because cold fuel flows through channels right behind it.
rocketEngine.info.injector.desc: The injector sprays fuel and oxygen into the chamber through dozens of small elements, mixing them into a fine mist so they burn evenly.
rocketEngine.info.injector.fact: Badly designed injectors can make the flame vibrate violently — engineers once tested them by setting off small explosions inside running engines.
rocketEngine.info.nozzle.desc: Below the throat the nozzle widens like a bell. The hot gas expands and speeds up to several kilometres per second, and pushing it out backwards pushes the rocket forwards.
rocketEngine.info.nozzle.fact: This is Newton's third law in action: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
rocketEngine.info.cooling_jacket.desc: Before it is burned, the fuel flows through channels along the chamber and nozzle walls. It soaks up heat and keeps the metal from melting — this is called regenerative cooling.
rocketEngine.info.cooling_jacket.fact: The heat the fuel picks up is not wasted: it goes back into the chamber when the fuel is burned.
rocketEngine.info.igniter.desc: The igniter starts the fire. Many kerosene engines inject a few drops of a chemical mix that bursts into flame on its own when it touches oxygen.
rocketEngine.info.igniter.fact: That self-igniting mix burns with a bright green flash — you can see it in many launch videos.
rocketEngine.info.gimbal.desc: The gimbal is a pivot joint at the top of the engine. It lets the whole engine tilt a few degrees, so the rocket can steer by pointing its thrust.
rocketEngine.info.gimbal.fact: Rockets steer more like a broom balanced on your hand than like a car — the engine keeps moving under the rocket to stop it tipping over.
rocketEngine.info.thrust_frame.desc: The thrust frame carries the engine's huge push into the body of the rocket. It must be strong, but as light as possible.
rocketEngine.info.thrust_frame.fact: A medium-sized rocket engine can push with the weight of around 80 cars.
rocketEngine.info.actuators.desc: Two actuators — powerful pistons — push and pull on the engine to tilt it on its gimbal, one for each direction.
rocketEngine.info.actuators.fact: They correct the engine’s angle many times every second while the rocket climbs.
rocketEngine.info.turbine.desc: Hot gas spins the turbine wheel at tens of thousands of turns per minute. The turbine shares one shaft with the pumps and drives them.
rocketEngine.info.turbine.fact: A rocket turbopump can be as powerful as a large ship’s engine, yet small enough to carry in your arms.
rocketEngine.info.fuel_pump.desc: The fuel pump takes kerosene from the tank and raises its pressure so it can be forced through the cooling channels and into the chamber.
rocketEngine.info.fuel_pump.fact: The pressure it makes is hundreds of times higher than the air pressure around you.
rocketEngine.info.lox_pump.desc: The oxygen pump moves liquid oxygen at about −183 °C into the injector. Burning needs oxygen, and there is no air in space, so the rocket carries its own.
rocketEngine.info.lox_pump.fact: A rocket usually carries more than twice as much oxygen as fuel, by weight.
rocketEngine.info.gas_generator.desc: The gas generator burns a small amount of fuel and oxygen to make hot gas that drives the turbine. It is like a tiny rocket engine powering the big one.
rocketEngine.info.gas_generator.fact: It burns with extra fuel on purpose, so the gas is cool enough not to melt the turbine blades.
rocketEngine.info.turbine_exhaust.desc: After spinning the turbine, the gas is dumped overboard through this pipe. In a gas-generator engine this gas adds a little thrust.
rocketEngine.info.turbine_exhaust.fact: Its smoky, fuel-rich exhaust is the dark plume you often see next to the main flame.
rocketEngine.info.oxidizer_lines.desc: These pipes carry liquid oxygen from the tank into the pump and from the pump to the injector.
rocketEngine.info.oxidizer_lines.fact: Liquid oxygen is so cold that the pipes are often covered in frost before launch.
rocketEngine.info.main_oxidizer_valve.de: This valve opens and closes the flow of oxygen to the engine. Opening the valves in the right order is what starts and stops the engine safely.
rocketEngine.info.main_oxidizer_valve.fa: The whole start-up sequence takes only a few seconds and is run by the computer.
rocketEngine.info.fuel_lines.desc: These pipes carry kerosene from the tank to the fuel pump, and from the pump to the cooling channels at the bottom of the nozzle.
rocketEngine.info.fuel_lines.fact: The kerosene used in rockets is a very pure version of the fuel used in jet airliners.
rocketEngine.info.main_fuel_valve.desc: This valve controls the flow of fuel to the engine. Together with the oxygen valve it sets how strongly the engine burns.
rocketEngine.info.main_fuel_valve.fact: Some engines can be throttled down to less than half power to land a rocket gently.
rocketEngine.info.controller.desc: The engine controller is a computer that reads sensors for pressure, temperature and speed, and opens valves and moves actuators to keep the engine running safely.
rocketEngine.info.controller.fact: If something goes wrong, it can shut the engine down in a fraction of a second.

electricMotor.title: Electric motor
electricMotor.summary: A brushed DC motor: magnets, copper coils and a spinning switch that turn electricity into motion.
electricMotor.credit: Electric motor: an original design modelled by Hologemma (brushed DC motor).
electricMotor.info.housing.desc: The steel housing holds everything together. It also carries the magnetic field from one magnet round to the other, which makes the motor stronger.
electricMotor.info.housing.fact: Electric motors turn up to 90% or more of their electrical energy into motion — far more efficient than a petrol engine.
electricMotor.info.north_magnet.desc: Two permanent magnets face each other inside the housing, with their north and south poles pointing at the rotor. Together they make a strong magnetic field across the middle.
electricMotor.info.north_magnet.fact: Like poles push apart and opposite poles pull together — a motor is a machine that keeps using that push and pull.
electricMotor.info.south_magnet.desc: The south magnet sits opposite the north one. The magnetic field runs from north to south straight through the spinning rotor.
electricMotor.info.south_magnet.fact: Strong modern magnets are made from neodymium, a rare-earth metal.
electricMotor.info.shaft.desc: The steel shaft runs through the middle of the motor. The rotor is fixed to it, and its end sticks out to drive a wheel, a fan or a propeller.
electricMotor.info.shaft.fact: The turning force a motor produces at its shaft is called torque.
electricMotor.info.armature_core.desc: The armature core is a stack of thin iron sheets with teeth. The copper coils are wound around the teeth, and the iron makes their magnetic field much stronger.
electricMotor.info.armature_core.fact: It is made from thin insulated sheets, not solid iron, so that wasteful swirling currents (eddy currents) cannot heat it up.
electricMotor.info.windings.desc: When current flows through a coil it becomes an electromagnet. The magnets push one side of the coil and pull the other, so the rotor turns.
electricMotor.info.windings.fact: More turns of wire or more current make a stronger electromagnet — and more torque.
electricMotor.info.commutator.desc: The commutator is a ring of copper segments on the shaft, each joined to a coil. As the rotor turns it keeps switching which coils get current, so the push always continues in the same direction.
electricMotor.info.commutator.fact: Without the commutator the rotor would just turn half a turn, stop and rock back and forth.
electricMotor.info.brushes.desc: Two carbon blocks are pressed onto the commutator by springs. They slide on it as it spins and carry current from the battery into the coils.
electricMotor.info.brushes.fact: Brushes slowly wear away, which is why modern electric cars and drones use brushless motors controlled by electronics.
electricMotor.info.front_bearing.desc: A ball bearing lets the shaft spin smoothly with very little friction. Steel balls roll between an inner and an outer ring.
electricMotor.info.front_bearing.fact: Rolling is far easier than sliding — the same reason wheels were such a big invention.
electricMotor.info.rear_bearing.desc: The second bearing supports the other end of the shaft, so the rotor stays perfectly centred between the magnets.
electricMotor.info.rear_bearing.fact: The gap between the spinning rotor and the magnets is often less than a millimetre.
electricMotor.info.front_end_cap.desc: The front end cap closes the housing and holds the front bearing in place.
electricMotor.info.front_end_cap.fact: The vents in the caps let air flow through to cool the coils.
electricMotor.info.rear_end_cap.desc: The rear end cap holds the rear bearing and the brush holders that keep the brushes in position on the commutator.
electricMotor.info.rear_end_cap.fact: It is usually made of plastic or another insulator so the brushes are not short-circuited.
electricMotor.info.fan.desc: The fan spins with the shaft and blows air through the motor, carrying away heat from the coils.
electricMotor.info.fan.fact: Heat is the main thing that limits how hard you can push a motor.
electricMotor.info.terminals.desc: The terminals are where the battery wires connect. Swap the two wires and the motor spins the other way.
electricMotor.info.terminals.fact: The same motor can also work backwards as a generator: spin the shaft and it makes electricity.
electricMotor.hint.housing: The housing is the base of the motor.
electricMotor.hint.north_magnet: The magnets are glued inside the housing — place the housing first.
electricMotor.hint.south_magnet: The magnets are glued inside the housing — place the housing first.

skeleton.title: Human skeleton
skeleton.summary: The bones that hold you up and protect your organs — from the skull to the toes, in 34 parts.
skeleton.credit: Skeleton: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science, CC BY 4.0.
skeleton.info.sacrum.desc: The sacrum is a triangle-shaped bone at the bottom of the spine, made of five vertebrae that fuse together as you grow. It joins the spine to the hips and carries the weight of the upper body.
skeleton.info.sacrum.fact: Below it sits the coccyx, the tailbone — a tiny leftover of the tail our distant ancestors had.
skeleton.info.lumbar_spine.desc: The five lumbar vertebrae in the lower back are the biggest and strongest in the spine, because they carry the most weight. Soft discs between them absorb shocks.
skeleton.info.lumbar_spine.fact: Lower back pain is one of the most common health problems in the world — strong core muscles help protect these bones.
skeleton.info.thoracic_spine.desc: The twelve thoracic vertebrae form the middle of the back. Each one is joined to a pair of ribs, building the cage that protects the heart and lungs.
skeleton.info.thoracic_spine.fact: The spinal cord runs through a hole in every vertebra, like a cable through a stack of rings.
skeleton.info.cervical_spine.desc: The seven cervical vertebrae form the neck. The top two, the atlas and the axis, are special: they let your head nod and turn.
skeleton.info.cervical_spine.fact: A giraffe also has just seven neck vertebrae — they are simply much longer.
skeleton.info.cranium.desc: The cranium is the part of the skull that surrounds and protects the brain. It is made of eight bones joined by wavy seams called sutures.
skeleton.info.cranium.fact: A newborn baby's skull has soft gaps between the bones (fontanelles) so the head can squeeze through birth and the brain can grow.
skeleton.info.facial_bones.desc: The facial bones shape your face: the cheekbones, the upper jaw (maxilla), the nose bones and the walls of the eye sockets.
skeleton.info.facial_bones.fact: Your upper teeth are held in the maxilla, which does not move — all chewing comes from the lower jaw.
skeleton.info.mandible.desc: The mandible is the lower jaw, the only bone in the skull that moves. The small hyoid bone in the neck anchors the tongue.
skeleton.info.mandible.fact: The hyoid is the only bone in the body that does not connect to any other bone.
skeleton.info.ribs.desc: Twelve pairs of ribs curve around the chest. They protect the heart and lungs, and they move up and out each time you breathe in.
skeleton.info.ribs.fact: The bottom two pairs are "floating ribs": they are not attached to the sternum at the front.
skeleton.info.sternum.desc: The sternum, or breastbone, is a flat bone in the middle of the chest. The ribs attach to it with flexible cartilage.
skeleton.info.sternum.fact: In CPR you press on the sternum to squeeze the heart behind it.
skeleton.info.clavicle.desc: The clavicle, or collarbone, is a slim bone that holds the shoulder out to the side so the arm can move freely.
skeleton.info.clavicle.fact: It is one of the most commonly broken bones, often from falling onto an outstretched hand.
skeleton.info.scapula.desc: The scapula, or shoulder blade, is a flat triangular bone on the back. Seventeen muscles attach to it and move the arm.
skeleton.info.scapula.fact: It is held to the body almost only by muscles, which is why the shoulder can move so far in every direction.
skeleton.info.humerus.desc: The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm. Its round head fits into a shallow socket on the scapula to form the shoulder joint.
skeleton.info.humerus.fact: The 'funny bone' is not a bone: it is a nerve passing over the bottom of the humerus at the elbow.
skeleton.info.radius.desc: The radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side. It can roll around the ulna, which lets you turn your palm up and down.
skeleton.info.radius.fact: A broken wrist is very often a break at the end of the radius.
skeleton.info.ulna.desc: The ulna is the forearm bone on the little-finger side. Its top end forms the point of your elbow.
skeleton.info.ulna.fact: Together the radius and ulna let the forearm both bend and twist.
skeleton.info.hand.desc: Each hand has 27 bones: 8 small wrist bones (carpals), 5 palm bones (metacarpals) and 14 finger bones (phalanges).
skeleton.info.hand.fact: Your two hands contain about a quarter of all the bones in your body.
skeleton.info.hip_bone.desc: The hip bone is a large, curved bone made of three bones fused together (ilium, ischium and pubis). The two hip bones and the sacrum form the pelvis.
skeleton.info.hip_bone.fact: The deep socket where the thigh bone fits is called the acetabulum — Latin for 'vinegar cup'.
skeleton.info.femur.desc: The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone in the body. It runs from the hip to the knee.
skeleton.info.femur.fact: It is roughly a quarter of your height — doctors can estimate how tall someone was from the femur alone.
skeleton.info.patella.desc: The patella, or kneecap, sits inside the tendon at the front of the knee. It protects the joint and gives the thigh muscles better leverage.
skeleton.info.patella.fact: Babies are born with kneecaps made of cartilage that only turns into bone over the first years of life.
skeleton.info.tibia.desc: The tibia, or shinbone, is the large bone of the lower leg that carries your weight from the knee to the ankle.
skeleton.info.tibia.fact: You can feel its front edge right under the skin of your shin — that is why a knock there hurts so much.
skeleton.info.fibula.desc: The fibula is the thin bone beside the tibia. It carries little weight but anchors muscles and forms the outer ankle bone.
skeleton.info.fibula.fact: Surgeons sometimes use a piece of the fibula to rebuild a damaged jaw.
skeleton.info.foot.desc: Each foot has 26 bones that form arches. The arches act like springs, spreading your weight and absorbing the shock of every step.
skeleton.info.foot.fact: The calcaneus, the heel bone, is the largest bone in the foot.
skeleton.hint.sacrum: The sacrum is the base of the skeleton.
skeleton.hint.lumbar_spine: The lumbar spine stands on the sacrum — place the sacrum first.
skeleton.hint.thoracic_spine: The thoracic spine sits above the lumbar spine — place the lumbar spine first.
skeleton.hint.cervical_spine: The neck sits on top of the thoracic spine — place the thoracic spine first.
skeleton.hint.cranium: The skull balances on the top of the neck — place the cervical spine first.
skeleton.hint.facial_bones: The face bones attach to the front of the cranium — place the cranium first.
skeleton.hint.mandible: The lower jaw hinges on the skull — place the cranium first.
skeleton.hint.ribs: Every rib joins a thoracic vertebra at the back — place the thoracic spine first.
skeleton.hint.sternum: The sternum closes the ribcage at the front — place both sets of ribs first.
skeleton.hint.clavicle: The collarbone joins the top of the sternum — place the sternum first.
skeleton.hint.scapula: The shoulder blade connects to the collarbone and rests on the ribs — place those first.
skeleton.hint.humerus: The upper arm fits into the shoulder socket on the scapula — place the scapula first.
skeleton.hint.forearm: The forearm bones meet the humerus at the elbow — place the humerus first.
skeleton.hint.hand: The wrist joins both forearm bones — place the radius and ulna first.
skeleton.hint.hip_bone: The hip bones join the sacrum at the back — place the sacrum first.
skeleton.hint.femur: The thigh bone fits into the hip socket — place the hip bone first.
skeleton.hint.patella: The kneecap sits on the front of the femur — place the femur first.
skeleton.hint.tibia: The shinbone meets the femur at the knee — place the femur first.
skeleton.hint.fibula: The fibula is tied to the side of the tibia — place the tibia first.
skeleton.hint.foot: The ankle joins the tibia and fibula — place both first.
muscles.title: Human muscles
muscles.summary: The major muscle groups that move your body — from the face and jaw to the toes — built onto the skeleton.
muscles.credit: Muscles: BodyParts3D (CC BY 4.0) and Z-Anatomy (CC BY-SA 4.0); this model is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0.
muscles.info.skeleton_base.desc: The skeleton is the frame the muscles pull on. Muscles are fixed to bones by tendons; when a muscle shortens, it pulls a bone and moves a joint.
muscles.info.skeleton_base.fact: Muscles can only pull, never push — that is why they work in opposite pairs.
muscles.info.intercostals.desc: The intercostal muscles fill the spaces between the ribs. They lift and lower the ribcage, helping you breathe.
muscles.info.intercostals.fact: Different layers run in crossing directions, like the layers of plywood.
muscles.info.diaphragm.desc: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, air is drawn into the lungs.
muscles.info.diaphragm.fact: Hiccups are sudden, involuntary twitches of the diaphragm.
muscles.info.back_muscles.desc: The deep back muscles run along the spine; quadratus lumborum joins the lowest rib to the pelvis. They keep you upright, bend you backwards and sideways and twist your back.
muscles.info.back_muscles.fact: They are working almost all the time you are awake, even when you just stand still.
muscles.info.pelvic_floor.desc: The pelvic floor is a hammock of muscles across the bottom of the pelvis. It supports the organs of the belly and helps control the bladder and bowel.
muscles.info.pelvic_floor.fact: You use it every time you cough or laugh, to stop pressure pushing things downwards.
muscles.info.neck_muscles.desc: Neck muscles hold up and turn the head — about 5 kg — and help you swallow and breathe. The big sternocleidomastoid runs from behind the ear to the collarbone.
muscles.info.neck_muscles.fact: Looking down at a phone makes the head feel several times heavier to these muscles.
muscles.info.rhomboids.desc: The rhomboids sit between the shoulder blades. They pull the shoulder blades together and towards the spine.
muscles.info.rhomboids.fact: They help you keep good posture and stop your shoulders rolling forward.
muscles.info.trapezius.desc: The trapezius is a large kite-shaped muscle across the upper back and neck. It lifts, lowers and rotates the shoulder blades.
muscles.info.trapezius.fact: You use its top part every time you shrug your shoulders.
muscles.info.abdominal_wall.desc: The abdominal wall has four muscles: the rectus abdominis (the "six-pack") at the front and three layers on the sides — external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis. They bend and twist the trunk and squeeze the belly to protect the organs and help you breathe out hard.
muscles.info.abdominal_wall.fact: The "six-pack" look comes from bands of tendon that cross the rectus abdominis — everyone has them, but fat usually hides them.
muscles.info.hand_muscles.desc: Small muscles inside the hand make fine finger movements possible: spreading, closing, and bringing the thumb across the palm.
muscles.info.hand_muscles.fact: Most finger strength actually comes from forearm muscles pulling on long tendons, like puppet strings.
muscles.info.foot_muscles.desc: Small muscles in the foot support its arches and move the toes, helping you balance and push off when you walk.
muscles.info.foot_muscles.fact: Walking barefoot works these little muscles much more than walking in shoes.
muscles.info.rotator_cuff.desc: Four muscles wrap around the shoulder joint and hold the ball of the humerus in its shallow socket while the arm moves.
muscles.info.rotator_cuff.fact: Throwing a ball hard puts huge strain on these muscles — rotator cuff injuries are common in sports.
muscles.info.pectoral.desc: The chest muscles — pectoralis major and minor, plus serratus anterior on the side of the ribs — pull the arm across the body and move the shoulder blade forward.
muscles.info.pectoral.fact: Serratus anterior looks like a row of fingers on the side of the ribs — boxers use it to punch.
muscles.info.deltoid.desc: The deltoid is the rounded muscle that caps the shoulder. Its three parts lift the arm forwards, sideways and backwards.
muscles.info.deltoid.fact: It is named after the Greek letter delta (Δ), because of its triangle shape.
muscles.info.biceps_brachii.desc: The biceps at the front of the upper arm bends the elbow and turns the palm up. The brachialis beneath it is the elbow’s strongest bender.
muscles.info.biceps_brachii.fact: The biceps works hardest when you turn a screwdriver clockwise — the reason most screws tighten that way.
muscles.info.triceps.desc: The triceps at the back of the upper arm straightens the elbow. It works opposite the biceps.
muscles.info.triceps.fact: It makes up about two thirds of the muscle in the upper arm.
muscles.info.forearm_flexors.desc: The forearm flexors on the palm side bend the wrist and fingers and turn the palm down. You use them to grip.
muscles.info.forearm_flexors.fact: Watch the inside of your forearm while you wiggle your fingers — you can see these muscles move.
muscles.info.forearm_extensors.desc: The forearm extensors on the back of the forearm straighten the wrist and fingers and help turn the palm up.
muscles.info.forearm_extensors.fact: "Tennis elbow" is pain where these muscles attach at the outside of the elbow.
muscles.info.hip_flexors.desc: The iliopsoas runs from the lower spine and the inside of the pelvis to the thigh bone. It lifts the knee towards the chest.
muscles.info.hip_flexors.fact: It is the only muscle that connects the spine directly to the leg.
muscles.info.gluteals.desc: The gluteal muscles form the buttock. They straighten the hip, keep the pelvis level while you walk, and rotate the thigh.
muscles.info.gluteals.fact: Gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the human body.
muscles.info.adductors.desc: The adductors on the inside of the thigh pull the legs together and help steady the hip.
muscles.info.adductors.fact: Riders use them to grip a horse with their knees.
muscles.info.quadriceps.desc: The four quadriceps muscles at the front of the thigh straighten the knee — for standing up, kicking and jumping. Sartorius crosses diagonally over them.
muscles.info.quadriceps.fact: Sartorius is the longest muscle in the body.
muscles.info.hamstrings.desc: The three hamstrings at the back of the thigh bend the knee and straighten the hip. They are key for running.
muscles.info.hamstrings.fact: Sprinters often pull a hamstring because these muscles work very hard to slow the leg at full speed.
muscles.info.calf.desc: The calf muscles — gastrocnemius and soleus — lift the heel and push you forwards with every step. Deeper muscles curl the toes.
muscles.info.calf.fact: They join the Achilles tendon, the thickest and strongest tendon in the body.
muscles.info.shin.desc: The shin muscles at the front and side of the lower leg lift the foot and toes and turn the foot outwards.
muscles.info.shin.fact: When they are weak or tired, the toes can catch on the ground and trip you.
